prize_parts.citation: for developing targeted protein degradation by heterobifunctional molecules, in which designed small molecules bring a chosen protein and an E3 ubiquitin ligase together so that the protein is destroyed

statement.case_for: After the first round I still place targeted protein degradation first, and I think the case has become clearer. Members from several backgrounds, including Brzezinski, Zou, Somfai, Sparr and Linke, accept that induced proximity is a genuine new principle: a small molecule is designed to bring a target and an E3 ligase together, so the protein is removed rather than occupied. The chemistry is designable and testable with an unambiguous readout (degradation kinetics, ternary-complex cooperativity, E3 dependence), and independent groups routinely make and validate degraders against targets that have no conventional active site. Crews and Deshaies supply the concept and first proofs; Ciulli's structure-guided VHL ligands and ternary-complex work turned it into rational, drug-like chemistry. I would word the citation around the induced-proximity mechanism and the chemical design of heterobifunctional degraders, not around the clinical pipeline, so it stands even if approvals arrive later.
statement.case_against: No PROTAC is approved, so the medical payoff is promised and not demonstrated, and a prize now could be judged early. The three-name limit forces a cut that cannot be made clean: Sakamoto shares the 2001 proof of concept, and Handa, Ito and Gray are central to the cereblon and glue strand that a PROTAC-centred citation leaves out. Chabes is right that the shared E3-redirection mechanism links the two strands, and if the committee prefers a mechanism-first prize, my configuration undercredits cereblon. Finally, B057 is more mature and has cleaner credit, and B068 is the more crowded case.

responses.point: Chabes holds that PROTACs and cereblon-based glues share one mechanism, an E3 ligase redirected to a new substrate by a small molecule, so one citation can cover both, with Handa in the third place instead of Ciulli.
responses.response: This is the strongest challenge to my configuration and I have thought about it carefully. The shared mechanism is real, and Handa's identification of cereblon is what made the glue strand chemically understandable. But the two strands arose by different routes. PROTACs were designed from the start as bifunctional molecules, whereas glues were found in thalidomide-type drugs and rationalised afterwards. A citation broad enough to cover both would say little about what was actually achieved, and the Chabes trio leaves out the structure-guided design chemistry that made degraders general. I therefore keep Ciulli and keep the wording on designed heterobifunctional degraders. I would accept a mechanism-first wording that mentions induced proximity, but I would not drop Ciulli for Handa.

responses.point: Sparr says the PROTAC versus glue split and the three-person limit work against B068 more than against B022, and that she sees B068 as medicinal chemistry more than a new chemical concept.
responses.response: The attribution point is fair, and it is the main reason I call the B068 cut contestable. I do not think it makes the case fail. The three-person limit constrains every shortlisted part, and B022 has the same issue with Pappu and Mittag. As to concept, I would say the new idea is a chemical one: ternary-complex cooperativity, linker design and E3 choice give design rules that transfer across targets, much as ligand design did in catalysis. On your condensate preference, I accept that Rosen's multivalency work is quantitatively chemical. My remaining hesitation about B022 is that its main impact is a new description of cells, whereas degraders add a new class of molecules.

responses.point: Somfai and Zou put Pd-catalysed C-N coupling first because it is general, fully mature and cleanly credited to Buchwald and Hartwig, and Somfai would acknowledge Kosugi and Migita in the background.
responses.response: I agree B057 is the safest choice on maturity and credit, and it is my first alternative. Your answer on novelty, that amine binding and C-N reductive elimination needed their own ligand and mechanistic solution, is a good one, and I take it more seriously than I did in round 1. My preference stays with B068 because I think a prize now should honour a new capability and not a second major method in a family the 2010 prize already honoured. If the committee decides that maturity and clean credit outweigh novelty, I could support B057 as a shared final choice, with a citation that says general and catalytic so that the Kosugi and Migita precedent is handled.

responses.point: Linke, as chair, asks whether a two-part configuration or a shared first choice could draw more support than the four single-ballot positions, and prefers B022 with B057 and B068 as alternatives.
responses.response: Since you and I both list B068 and B057 as fallbacks in some form, I think a shared single first choice is more plausible than a two-part prize, because two parts would add names to a field where credit is already contested. I would rather argue the single case than build a package. I would also say that your own concern about in-cell relevance of condensates is a reason to wait for B022. I do not think B068 faces the same problem, since its central claim, that the target is degraded, is measured directly in cells and reproduced widely.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will award B068 before any degrader is approved, and whether the timing risk should outweigh the principle.
Whether a three-name cut among Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli, Sakamoto, Handa, Ito and Gray can be defended, and whether the cereblon glue strand should have been given a place.
Whether C-N coupling is a distinct enough advance from the 2010 prize to be preferred over a newer principle; I am not a synthetic chemist and rely on colleagues' judgment.
My knowledge of the clinical status of degraders is from general knowledge and was not independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My postdoc mentors (Stevens, Boey) and Linkoping colleagues are not credited on any shortlisted ballot, and none of the shortlisted candidates is a close collaborator. I note only a loose thematic proximity of my biosensor and bioengineering work to nanoparticle and delivery topics such as B054, which is not in my configuration. No recusal is indicated.
